generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, it is easy to assume creativity belongs to the arts and that serious study is only method and evidence. In fact academic work across disciplines runs on creative thinking: a good question, a fresh connection between findings, and a way of seeing a problem that others missed all begin with someone generating ideas. Creativity here is a skill you build alongside your other methods, not a gift you either have or lack.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students given the same open essay, each free to choose a question worth exploring.

Student A picks the first question that comes to mind, the one the tutor used as an example, and writes it up. The task is done, safely. But Student A settled on a single obvious question without looking for others, treating creativity as something the essay did not really need. This is the fixed view of creativity.

Student B jots down several possible questions first, including a few that seem unlikely, then finds an angle that links two of them in a way the reading had not suggested. The question that results is their own. This is creativity as a skill: generate options, make a connection, then choose.

Both students finished the essay. Only Student B treated creativity as something to practise, turning a safe question into one of their own.
generatedProse.summary: Across any subject, creativity is a skill you can build, not a gift reserved for a few: it means generating ideas, connecting what you find, and seeing a question from more than one angle. You can now explain what creativity is and recognise it in how a student approaches a task. The next lessons turn this into practice: the two modes of thinking behind creative work, and the barriers that get in the way.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's approach creative rather than fixed?

items.text: They generated several possible questions and connected two into an angle of their own.
They chose the question the tutor had already used.
They finished the essay more quickly than Student A.
They waited until they felt naturally inspired.

feedback.correct: That's right. Generating several questions and connecting two into an angle of their own is creativity as a skill.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B did with their ideas, beyond finishing the essay.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B was creative by generating several questions and connecting two into an angle of their own, not by being fast or waiting for inspiration.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject.
